sections.h2: Which Dearborn office sends the tax bill?
sections.html:
The city's own Treasury Division does. Dearborn lies in Wayne County, yet the city sends the bill and takes the payment, at the cashier's counter in the Dearborn Administrative Center, 16901 Michigan Avenue, weekdays from eight to half past four.

Valuation is a separate office. The Assessing Department in Suite 5 of the same building sets every parcel's value yearly, answers at 313-943-2140 and keeps weekday hours of eight to five. Email and voicemail get a reply within 48 hours, and in all cases within seven business days.

Deed copies live elsewhere. The Wayne County Register of Deeds, International Building, 400 Monroe, sixth floor, Detroit, holds them, and owners who need liber and page numbers go there.

Two bills arrive each year. The summer levy is struck on July 1 and falls due September 14. The winter levy is struck on December 1 and falls due February 14.

Dearborn's two property tax bills
BillLevy datePayment deadlineContents
SummerJuly 1September 14, or three installments on Sept. 14, Nov. 14 and Jan. 14School, city and county-allocated operating taxes
WinterDecember 1February 14, in one paymentThe balance of county taxes plus city Combined Sewer Overflow debt

Splitting the summer bill into installments costs a single $3 fee, and a deferral application exists for eligible residents. Winter tax has no installment option at all.

A postmark earns nothing. Dearborn books a payment on the day the money arrives, so a check in the mail late is a late payment. The 24-hour drop box in the lot facing the Administrative Center's main doors is the safer route near a deadline.

Five routes exist, and they differ in cost.

  • Online through BS&A: free for an owner who registers the parcel, with a 3% fee on cards and $3 on an e-check. A tenant who is not the owner pays $6 to set up an account.
  • The DivDat app and the lobby kiosk: cards carry 3%, while e-checks through the app cost nothing.
  • By mail: write the account and parcel numbers on the check and send it to City of Dearborn, Tax Dept. 3102, P.O. Box 30516, Lansing, MI 48909-8016. Certified mail must instead go to the Administrative Center.
  • Automatic ACH debit: free, and you can cancel any time.
  • In person: the cashier's counter, or the drop box outside.

If a closing lands close to a deadline, have the title company pay out of the seller's proceeds by a method that posts that same day.

sections.h2: Why does a Dearborn sale change the next tax bill?
sections.html:
Because the cap resets. Assessed value is half of estimated market value, and Michigan's formula multiplies taxable value, divided by 1,000, by the millage rate. Since Proposal A passed in 1994, an owner's taxable value can grow each year only by inflation or 5%, whichever is lower.

That limit stops applying in the year after ownership transfers. Taxable value then jumps up to assessed value, so the new owner's first bill may sit far above the seller's old one.

Sellers of long-held homes should know this before they talk price with buyers, since buyers will estimate their bill from the uncapped number. Be ready to explain it when a buyer asks why the tax will change.

sections.h2: Is the assessment notice a tax bill?
sections.html:
No. The yearly Change of Assessment Notice arrives by mail ahead of the March board and only reports movement in assessed and taxable value. The dates, times and places of the March Board of Review are printed on it, so keep it until the hearing season ends.

Two kinds of property get assessed: real property, meaning buildings and land, and personal property, meaning the items a business uses to operate. The assessor weighs building size and location, construction materials, lot size, additions, land improvements and any damage or construction work. A homeowner can also compare a parcel's record against the city's residential assessment database, which is searchable online.

Check the record card for errors such as the wrong number of bathrooms or a finished basement that does not exist. Verifying that the record card is accurate is the first step to take.

sections.h2: How to appeal your assessment or request an exemption
sections.html:
Call the Assessing Department first. Plenty of disputes turn out to be a wrong square footage or a misread fact that staff can fix on the spot. When that fails, file with the March Board of Review, the only yearly window to contest value, and one that covers only the current year.

Bring photos, an appraisal or comparable sales along with the petition. A residential owner unhappy with the result can then petition the Michigan Tax Tribunal, though the March board comes first for houses. Commercial and industrial owners may go straight to the tribunal.

  • Principal Residence Exemption: removes up to 18 mills of local school operating tax when the owner lives in the house.
  • Low-income exemption: relief at 50% of value under MCL 211.7u, with the application and documents due by the final December Board of Review session.
  • Disabled veteran exemption: affidavit Form 5107 goes in between January 1 and December 31, with VA proof; a December 30 postmark counts.

sections.h2: What buyers and sellers file after a Dearborn closing
sections.html:
The assessor expects forms from both sides. The buyer owes a Property Transfer Affidavit within 45 days, and being late costs $5 a day, capped at $200 for a house. It is required even if no deed is ever recorded.

The seller who claimed the principal residence exemption sends Form 2602, a request to rescind it, effective on closing day. A buyer who will live in the house sends Form 2368 to claim the exemption, along with a Name and Address Change form.

Unpaid bills are a separate matter. Call the city treasury and the Wayne County Treasurer for exact payoff figures before closing, including penalties and the point where collection moves from the city to the county. If taxes are owed, the title company normally pays them from the seller's proceeds at closing, so ask for the payoff figure early. The title company can also tell you whether the summer or winter bill is the next one due, which decides how much of the year's tax you owe as the seller.

Dearborn is an inner-ring suburb bordering Detroit, with compact lots in about 24.25 square miles and roughly 105,611 residents. The typical owned home is valued at $218,800, and owners live in 68.4% of occupied homes. Median rent is $1,327, and owners pay a median $1,672 monthly with a mortgage or $764 without. Older homes draw questions about roofs, plumbing and wiring, and the Assessing Department lets owners view record cards during business hours.

faqs.q: What is the Dearborn summer tax deadline?
faqs.a: September 14. The bill can be paid in three installments, on September 14, November 14 and January 14, for a single $3 fee.

faqs.q: Does Dearborn offer installments on winter taxes?
faqs.a: No. The winter bill is levied December 1 and must be paid whole by February 14.

faqs.q: Will the city honor a postmark on a mailed tax check?
faqs.a: No, the payment counts on the day the city receives it. A 24-hour drop box in the Administrative Center lot is the alternative.

faqs.q: Where do I begin if I think my Dearborn assessment is wrong?
faqs.a: With the Assessing Department, then the March Board of Review. A residential owner still unsatisfied can go on to the Michigan Tax Tribunal.

faqs.q: What must a buyer file with the city after closing on a Dearborn house?
faqs.a: A Property Transfer Affidavit within 45 days, plus Form 2368 if the buyer will live there and wants the principal residence exemption.
